input_signals.name: AccrualsUnderDisinvestment
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), INDICATOR(SUB(dp, capx), 0))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accruals are most diagnostic of earnings manipulation when the firm is not investing: when depreciation exceeds capital expenditure the productive asset base is contracting, so any accrual-driven asset or earnings growth is purely accounting in nature and should reverse strongly.
input_signals.reasoning: The dp-versus-capx comparison is a clean, scale-free investment-regime switch that separates shrinking real capital from expanding real capital, and it interacts with accruals in the direction the economic story predicts. Firms replacing capital at or above depreciation can legitimately carry higher accruals from growing operations, so their accruals should be less informative. This conditional design tests whether the accrual anomaly is state-dependent on real investment rather than universal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), 1 ), indicator( sub( dp, capx ), 0 ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationLagBehindCapacity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, ppegt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that expand gross property, plant and equipment while simultaneously slowing their depreciation rate are capitalizing and under-expensing the new capital, so reported earnings overstate the economics of the investment and returns subsequently disappoint.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces a genuinely new accrual channel — depreciation policy, the largest non-working-capital accrual — rather than the receivables/inventory channel already tested, and ties it mechanically to the real investment being made. The multiplicative rank form concentrates the short leg on firms where both conditions hold, so gross-PPE growth alone or depreciation-rate declines alone are not sufficient to enter the extreme portfolios. It tests whether the "accounting versus productive growth" story operates through expense timing as well as through working capital.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( dp, ppegt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsWithExternalFinancing
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), SUMRANK(RATIO(sstk, LAG(at, 1)), GROWTH(dltt, 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accrual-inflated earnings are most damaging when the firm is simultaneously raising outside equity and debt, because managers have both the incentive to inflate reported growth and the ability to fund an expansion that internal cash flow cannot support.
input_signals.reasoning: This shifts the economic channel from the composition of assets to the financing of growth, which is the mechanism the anomaly literature associates with the strongest reversals and which none of the archive signals touches. Nested SUMRANK keeps all three legs on a common robust rank scale, avoiding the outlier problems that broke the level-space signals while still giving a fully ordered, densely populated cross-section for portfolio sorting. A weak result here would tell us the interaction is about asset composition, not funding.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), sumrank( ratio( sstk, lag( at, 1 ) ), growth( dltt, 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: NonCashWCAccrualPerGrossInvestment
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), ADD(capx, dp)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The sharpest reversals come from firms whose expansion is almost entirely non-cash working capital build measured against the scale of their genuine capital activity; one dollar of receivable and inventory accrual per dollar of gross real investment is accounting growth with no productive counterpart.
input_signals.reasoning: This deliberately merges the two constructions that independently produced reliable FF5 alpha — the properly cash- and debt-adjusted non-cash working capital numerator (t=−4.25) and the gross-investment denominator that delivered the best Sharpe (−0.264) — while keeping the level form that rank transforms destroyed. Scaling by capx+dp rather than lagged assets makes the denominator a direct measure of real investment intensity, so the ratio literally reads as accounting growth per unit of productive growth. If both alpha and slope improve, this becomes the consolidation anchor for later generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( sub( delta( act, 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), sub( delta( lct, 1 ), delta( dlc, 1 ) ) ), add( capx, dp ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: SoftAssetAmplifiedAccruals
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), RATIO(SUB(at, ADD(ppent, che)), at))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accruals are only as distortive as the balance sheet is discretionary: the same accrual load is far more likely to reverse in a firm whose assets are mostly soft (neither hard capital nor cash) because that is where managerial estimation latitude and unverifiable asset values reside.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the failed 0/1 disinvestment mask with a continuous, bounded amplifier — the share of assets that is neither PPE nor cash — so the cross-section stays fully ordered and no degenerate point mass sits at the decile breakpoints. It tests a distinct economic channel, accounting discretion capacity rather than growth composition, and both inputs are levels, consistent with the finding that magnitude information carries the alpha. The amplifier lies in roughly [0,1], so it modulates rather than dominates the accrual signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), 1 ), ratio( sub( at, add( ppent, che ) ), at ) )

input_signals.name: ExpansionCashFlowDeficit
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, DELTA(invt, 1)), oancf), LAG(at, 1)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is whether the firm's combined real and inventory expansion exceeds the operating cash flow available to fund it; a large expansion cash deficit means the growth is being carried by accruals and outside capital and must be unwound.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes the economic channel from asset composition to the funding gap between committed expansion and internally generated cash, which is the mechanism behind both the accrual and investment anomalies but has not yet been measured directly in the archive. It uses only three widely reported items so coverage should exceed the 0.076–0.089 range of the cash-flow-component signals, and it keeps the winsorized level form associated with real alpha. Firms whose capex and inventory build are fully cash-covered sit at the long end, which is economically the correct comparison group.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( add( capx, delta( invt, 1 ) ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: ThreeYearExpansionCashDeficit
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(capx, DELTA(invt, 1)), oancf), 3), LAG(at, 1)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that have run a cumulative three-year deficit between committed expansion (capital expenditure plus inventory build) and operating cash flow have financed growth with accruals and outside capital for long enough that the accounting overstatement is systematic, not transitory, and the reversal is correspondingly large.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the only mechanism with strong dual evidence (the expansion cash deficit, FMB −2.83 / α −4.1%) with the only construction change that clearly lifted alpha (three-year cumulation, which took α from −4.3% to −6.8%). Crucially the denominator stays lagged total assets rather than a cumulative capex flow, so the fragile small-denominator problem that flattened the ThreeYear slope is avoided. This is the leading consolidation candidate for the remaining generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( add( capx, delta( invt, 1 ) ), oancf ), 3 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: CumulativeAccrualLessCapexScaled
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)), at), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Over a three-year window, the excess of cumulative accruals over cumulative real capital spending measures how much of a firm's reported growth was booked rather than built, and this excess predicts returns negatively.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates exactly one design choice against ThreeYearAccrualPerCapexFlow (α −6.8%, FMB −0.54): the two limbs are differenced and scaled by total assets instead of being divided by each other, so no observation can explode when capex plus depreciation is near zero. If the slope turns strongly negative while alpha stays near −5% or better, we will have confirmed that every FMB failure in this archive is a denominator-tail artifact rather than economic non-monotonicity, which would let later generations trust level ratios throughout.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( ts_sum( sub( ib, oancf ), 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ), at ), 1 )

input_signals.name: AcquiredGrowthCashDeficit
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, aqc), oancf), LAG(at, 1)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Expansion through acquisition is the growth channel most prone to accounting overstatement, since acquired assets enter at negotiated fair values rather than at cost incurred; when total expansion including acquisitions outruns operating cash flow, subsequent returns are lowest.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive signal has measured real investment as organic capex, inventory or PPE, leaving the acquisition channel untested even though it is where "accounting growth" is most literal. Nesting it inside the funding-deficit form that already produced dual evidence lets us attribute any change in performance to the acquisition limb rather than to a new construction. Coverage is the diagnostic here, since aqc is sparsely reported for non-acquirers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( add( capx, aqc ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: SoftAssetAmplifiedCashDeficit
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, DELTA(invt, 1)), oancf), LAG(at, 1)), 1), RATIO(SUB(at, ADD(ppent, che)), at))
input_signals.hypothesis: A cash-financed expansion deficit is most likely to be reversed when the balance sheet absorbing it is soft — neither hard capital nor cash — because that is where the deficit can be parked in discretionary, unverifiable asset values.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the two mechanisms with the strongest and most similar cross-sectional slopes (expansion deficit, FMB −2.83; soft-asset-amplified accruals, FMB −3.20, Sharpe −0.271), testing whether they are the same effect or two independent conditions whose conjunction sharpens both legs. The amplifier is bounded roughly in [0,1] and continuous, so unlike the failed indicator mask it modulates without creating a point mass at the decile breakpoints. If the interaction beats both parents, discretion capacity becomes a general conditioning variable for later refinements.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( sub( add( capx, delta( invt, 1 ) ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ), 1 ), ratio( sub( at, add( ppent, che ) ), at ) )

input_signals.name: AccountingAssetCreationPerRealInvestment
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(ib, oancf), DELTA(intan, 1)), ADD(capx, dp)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Total non-cash asset creation has two accounting limbs — accruals from operations and capitalized intangibles — and their combined size relative to gross real investment measures how much of the balance sheet grew by recognition rather than by expenditure.
input_signals.reasoning: Capitalized intangibles are a recognition choice with no cash counterpart in the current period, economically parallel to accruals but entirely absent from the archive, so pooling them tests whether the reversal mechanism is about accruals specifically or about non-cash recognition generally. Using the gross-investment denominator that produced reliable alpha keeps the comparison to AccrualsPerGrossInvestment interpretable: any improvement is attributable to the intangible limb. Intangible reporting is uneven, so coverage will indicate whether this channel can support a stable portfolio.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( add( sub( ib, oancf ), delta( intan, 1 ) ), add( capx, dp ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: TotalExpansionDeficitPerGrossInvestment
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, ADD(aqc, DELTA(invt, 1))), oancf), ADD(capx, dp)), 5)
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically complete measure is how far total expansion — organic capital spending, acquisitions and inventory build — outruns operating cash flow, expressed per dollar of genuine capital activity rather than per dollar of assets.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the two structural features that have separately produced the best evidence: the funding-deficit numerator (FMB −2.83 to −3.43 across two variants) and the gross-investment denominator that generated the largest alphas, with intermediate 5% winsorization as a compromise between slope stability and tail information. Scaling by capx+dp instead of assets means the signal reads as deficit per unit of real investment, so asset-light accounting growers sort to the short leg for the same economic reason they do in the alpha-king signal. Coverage should sit near 0.080 given the aqc limb, which is acceptable relative to the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( add( capx, add( aqc, delta( invt, 1 ) ) ), oancf ), add( capx, dp ) ), 5 )

input_signals.name: SoftAssetAmplified3YAccrualIntensity
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, dp), 3)), 5), RATIO(SUB(at, ADD(ppent, che)), at))
input_signals.hypothesis: Sustained accrual-heavy, investment-light growth reverses most violently when it is parked in soft assets, because only unverifiable, discretionary carrying values allow the overstatement to persist for three years before correcting.
input_signals.reasoning: The discretion amplifier improved both the slope and Sharpe of the one-year accrual signal (FMB −3.20, Sharpe −0.271) and of the deficit signal (FMB −2.87, Sharpe −0.423), so applying it to the highest-alpha base signal tests whether the two effects compound rather than substitute. The amplifier is bounded in roughly [0,1] and continuous, so it modulates the intensity ratio without creating point masses at decile breakpoints. A clear improvement over the base would establish discretion capacity as the general conditioning variable for the final generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( ib, oancf ), 3 ), ts_sum( add( capx, dp ), 3 ) ), 5 ), ratio( sub( at, add( ppent, che ) ), at ) )

input_signals.name: DeficitPlusAccrualIntensityZ
input_signals.expression: ADD(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, aqc), oancf), LAG(at, 1))), ZSCORE(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, dp), 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accounting growth is identified by two economically distinct symptoms — a current funding gap between total expansion and operating cash flow, and a multi-year record of accruals unmatched by real investment — and a firm exhibiting both is unambiguously growing on paper.
input_signals.reasoning: The two limbs are the archive's slope champion (FMB −3.43) and its alpha champion (α −6.8%, t −4.38), and they are conceptually independent: one is a current-year cash state, the other a cumulative composition measure. ZSCORE rather than RANK puts them on a comparable scale while preserving the magnitude information that rank transforms repeatedly destroyed here, so the composite can inherit the deficit limb's monotone middle and the intensity limb's informative extremes. This is the most direct test of whether the two forms of evidence can be obtained in one signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: add( zscore( ratio( sub( add( capx, aqc ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), zscore( ratio( ts_sum( sub( ib, oancf ), 3 ), ts_sum( add( capx, dp ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ThreeYearAcquiredDeficitPerGrossInvestment
input_signals.expression: RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(capx, aqc), oancf), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, dp), 3))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that has funded three years of combined organic and acquired expansion out of accruals and outside capital, measured per dollar of genuine capital activity rather than per dollar of assets, is the purest case of accounting growth and should show the largest reversal.
input_signals.reasoning: This assembles the three features that have each independently improved results — the acquisition-inclusive deficit numerator (FMB −3.43), the gross-investment denominator that produced every large alpha, and three-year cumulation that lifted alpha from −4.3% to −6.8% — into a single parsimonious ratio. Cumulating the deficit failed when scaled by assets (α −3.9%), so this specifically tests whether cumulation only pays off under investment-intensity scaling, which is a clean and interpretable design question. Both limbs cumulate over the same window, so the ratio is dimensionless and stable across the capex cycle.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( ts_sum( sub( add( capx, aqc ), oancf ), 3 ), ts_sum( add( capx, dp ), 3 ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationAdequacyAmplifiedAccruals
input_signals.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(dp, capx))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accruals matter most when replacement investment is inadequate: if depreciation exceeds capital expenditure the productive base is shrinking, so any accrual-supported earnings growth has no real counterpart and must reverse.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator version of this exact economic idea produced the archive's second-strongest slope (FMB −3.38) with zero alpha, and I now know the alpha failure came from the 0/1 mask piling half the universe at a single value rather than from tail treatment, so the continuous dp/capx amplifier is the correct repair. The amplifier scales the accrual signal smoothly by how far real investment falls short of depreciation, keeping the cross-section fully ordered and the extreme deciles economically homogeneous. If alpha now appears alongside the slope, disinvestment-conditioned accruals become a second consolidation candidate.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), ratio( dp, capx ) )

input_signals.name: IntangibleParkedDeficit
input_signals.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, aqc), oancf), LAG(at, 1)), RATIO(intan, at))
input_signals.hypothesis: An expansion cash deficit is most likely to be reversed when the resulting assets are intangible, because purchased goodwill and intangibles carry negotiated values with no verifiable productive capacity behind them and are the natural resting place for overstated growth.
input_signals.reasoning: The soft-asset amplifier (assets minus PPE minus cash) improved the deficit signal's Sharpe and slope, but soft assets pool receivables, inventory and intangibles together; sharpening the amplifier to intangible intensity tests which component of discretion actually carries the effect. This matters economically because the acquisition limb of the deficit mechanically creates intangibles, so the amplifier and numerator describe the same corporate action from two sides. If intangible intensity outperforms the broad soft-asset version, later refinements should condition on intangible rather than working-capital discretion.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ratio( sub( add( capx, aqc ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ), ratio( intan, at ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualsPlusCapitalWithoutLaborZ
input_signals.expression: ADD(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), ZSCORE(SUB(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), GROWTH(emp, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuine capacity expansion requires both capital and workers; gross plant growing faster than headcount, combined with high accruals, indicates costs being capitalized into fixed assets and earnings recognized ahead of real operating capability.
input_signals.reasoning: The labor channel has twice delivered large reliable alphas (−5.8%, −4.8%) with wrong-signed slopes, and with winsorization ruled out as the cause the remaining explanation is the raw scale mismatch of differencing an asset-scaled accrual level against a growth rate, which standardizing both limbs fixes directly. Replacing employment growth with the capital-minus-labor growth wedge also sharpens the economics: it isolates capital deepening unaccompanied by hiring, which is where capitalization of operating costs shows up. A successful slope here would validate the ZSCORE-composite construction used in signal 1.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: add( zscore( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ) ), zscore( sub( growth( ppegt, 1 ), growth( emp, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ThreeYearDepAdequacyAmplifiedAccruals
input_signals.expression: MUL(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 3), at), RATIO(TS_SUM(dp, 3), TS_SUM(capx, 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Three years of accumulated accruals, weighted by how far cumulative capital spending has fallen short of cumulative depreciation, identifies firms whose reported growth has persistently outrun a shrinking productive base.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the two most productive levers in the archive: the dense, strictly positive dp/capx amplifier that produced the best balance of slope and alpha (FMB −3.25, α −4.8%), and three-year cumulation, the only construction that has ever pushed alpha past −6%. Cumulating both limbs over the same window also stabilizes the amplifier, since single-year capex is lumpy and its inverse is the noisiest part of the gen-5 winner. If alpha lands near −6% with a slope near −3, this becomes the primary candidate for the final generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ratio( ts_sum( sub( ib, oancf ), 3 ), at ), ratio( ts_sum( dp, 3 ), ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ThreeChannelAccountingGrowthZ
input_signals.expression: ADD(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, aqc), oancf), LAG(at, 1))), ADD(ZSCORE(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, dp), 3))), ZSCORE(MUL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(dp, capx)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accounting growth leaves three separable traces — a current cash funding gap on total expansion, a multi-year accrual-to-investment imbalance, and current accruals under inadequate replacement investment — and a firm displaying all three is the most reliably mispriced.
input_signals.reasoning: The deficit limb carries the archive's most consistent slopes (−2.8 to −3.4) while the other two carry the alpha, so pooling all three tests whether diversification across symptoms raises reliability enough to offset the alpha dilution seen in the two-channel gen-5 composite. Every limb is dense and continuous, so no point mass can destabilize the extreme deciles, and standardization keeps any single limb from dominating. Coverage is the diagnostic: the intersection includes aqc, so anything materially below 0.075 would make this unattractive relative to signals 1 and 2.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: add( zscore( ratio( sub( add( capx, aqc ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), add( zscore( ratio( ts_sum( sub( ib, oancf ), 3 ), ts_sum( add( capx, dp ), 3 ) ) ), zscore( mul( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ), ratio( dp, capx ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ConjunctionMinDeficitIntensity
input_signals.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), ADD(capx, dp))), ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(ADD(capx, aqc), oancf), LAG(at, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is only convincingly growing on paper when accruals are large relative to real investment *and* total expansion outruns operating cash flow; requiring both conditions simultaneously should produce a cleaner short leg than averaging the two symptoms.
input_signals.reasoning: Additive composites let one strong limb drag a firm into the extreme decile even when the other limb contradicts it, which plausibly explains why the gen-5 two-channel composite had a strong slope but diluted alpha; taking the minimum of the standardized limbs enforces conjunction while keeping the signal continuous and free of point masses, unlike indicators. This is a genuinely different operator structure rather than a rescaling, and it tests whether the mispricing requires joint symptoms or merely an aggregate score. If MIN beats ADD, the final generations should build conjunctions instead of sums.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( zscore( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), add( capx, dp ) ) ), zscore( ratio( sub( add( capx, aqc ), oancf ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: UnexplainedPPEGrowthWithAccruals
input_signals.expression: ADD(ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ppegt, 1), capx), LAG(ppegt, 1))), ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross property growing faster than capital expenditure means fixed assets arrived through acquisition, revaluation or capitalized operating costs rather than through cash outlay; combined with high accruals this is balance-sheet expansion by recognition rather than by expenditure.
input_signals.reasoning: Every real-investment benchmark in the archive has treated capex and PPE growth as interchangeable measures of productive investment, whereas their difference is precisely the non-cash component of hard-asset growth — an untested channel that is conceptually the fixed-asset analogue of accruals. Both limbs are dense and standardized, following the amplifier lesson from IntangibleParkedDeficit, and using ppegt rather than intan avoids the sparsity that destroyed that signal's portfolio spread. A strong result would open capitalization of costs into hard assets as a refinement axis for the endgame.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: add( zscore( ratio( sub( delta( ppegt, 1 ), capx ), lag( ppegt, 1 ) ) ), zscore( ratio( sub( ib, oancf ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: ThreeYearWCAccrualPerGrossInvestment
input_signals.expression: RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), 3), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, dp), 3))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cumulative non-cash working capital build per dollar of gross real investment is the cleanest statement of the economic story — three years of receivables and inventory expansion with no productive counterpart — and should inherit the alpha of the cumulative-intensity form and the slope of the balance-sheet accrual measure.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive contains two largely independent alpha sources: the non-cash working capital accrual numerator (t=−4.25 in level form, FMB −3.05 when scaled by gross investment) and the three-year cumulative intensity construction (α −6.8%); this signal is the first to combine them, replacing the total-accrual numerator with the working-capital numerator inside the winning ratio. Because working capital accruals reverse mechanically within one to two years, cumulating them over three years measures chronic non-reversal, which is economically stronger than a single-year snapshot. Coverage should be near 0.11, the best in the archive, which also makes it the most robust candidate for final consolidation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( ts_sum( sub( sub( delta( act, 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), sub( delta( lct, 1 ), delta( dlc, 1 ) ) ), 3 ), ts_sum( add( capx, dp ), 3 ) )

input_signals.name: CapStockScaled3YWCAccruals
input_signals.expression: RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), 3), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), ppent))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cumulative non-cash working capital build measured against total productive capital is the most literal statement of the economic story — three years of receivables and inventory growth with no productive base to justify it — and should benefit from the capital-stock floor at least as much as total accruals did.
input_signals.reasoning: The working-capital numerator is the archive's second independent alpha source and its cumulative version already carries a respectable slope (FMB −2.28, α −3.2%) with the best coverage in the archive (0.112); replacing the fragile gross-investment denominator with the capital-stock floor that just lifted the total-accrual family by 60 basis points of alpha is the natural test of whether the improvement is numerator-independent. Because working capital accruals reverse mechanically, three-year cumulation measures chronic non-reversal rather than a snapshot. High coverage makes this the most robust option if its metrics land close to the leaders.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( ts_sum( sub( sub( delta( act, 1 ), delta( che, 1 ) ), sub( delta( lct, 1 ), delta( dlc, 1 ) ) ), 3 ), add( ts_sum( capx, 3 ), ppent ) )

input_signals.name: DoubleBoundedAmplifiedCapStockAccruals
input_signals.expression: MUL(MUL(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 3), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), ppent)), RATIO(TS_SUM(dp, 3), TS_SUM(ADD(capx, dp), 3))), RATIO(SUB(at, ADD(ppent, che)), at))
input_signals.hypothesis: The most reversal-prone firms satisfy three conditions at once: large accruals relative to productive capital, gross investment that is almost entirely replacement, and a balance sheet dominated by soft, discretionary assets in which the overstatement can be parked.
input_signals.reasoning: Both amplifiers are bounded in roughly [0,1] and dense across the universe, which is precisely the condition that separated the successful dp/capx and soft-asset amplifiers from the sparse intangible amplifier that destroyed portfolio spread; the soft-asset amplifier previously moved a base signal's slope from −0.54 to −2.03 at a cost of 2.6 points of alpha. Stacking two mild bounded amplifiers on the strongest base tests whether slope gains accumulate faster than alpha decays, which the single-amplifier evidence suggests. If it overshoots into low alpha, signal 1 remains the preferred version of this idea, so the pair is jointly informative.

input_signals.name: CapStockScaledExpansionDeficit
input_signals.expression: RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(ADD(capx, aqc), oancf), 3), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), ppent))
input_signals.hypothesis: Three years of expansion — organic plus acquired — funded beyond operating cash flow, measured against the productive capital the firm actually operates, identifies growth that was financed rather than earned and has no capital base to sustain it.
input_signals.reasoning: This fills the one untested cell in the archive's two-dimensional design space: the funding-deficit numerator owns the strongest and most consistent Fama-MacBeth slopes (−2.8 to −3.4 across five variants) while the capital-stock denominator owns the strongest alphas (−6.4% to −7.4%), and they have never been combined. Because the deficit numerator is monotone through the middle of the cross-section where the accrual-intensity numerator is flat, this is the most plausible route to a signal with both FMB near −3 and alpha near −6%. Coverage should be near 0.080 given the aqc limb, acceptable relative to the leaders.
